logline: After a virus carried by rainfall wipes out most of Scandinavia's population, Danish siblings Simone and Rasmus emerge from six years in a bunker to search for their missing scientist father - and the cure he may have left behind.

pull_quotes.text: The Rain is some of the best survivalist drama to hit screens in years, with exciting, unpredictable and genuinely likable characters.
The emotional journeys of the young people eking out a tense post-apocalyptic existence pulled me in much more than I was expecting.

seasons.review_body: The Rain Season 1 launched on Netflix in May 2018 as the platform's first Danish original series, arriving with a post-apocalyptic premise that grounded its science-fiction virus mythology in intimate character work. Produced by Miso Film, the eight-episode season follows siblings Simone and Rasmus - played by Alba August and Lucas Lynggaard Tonnesen - as they emerge from bunker isolation into a Scandinavia scoured by the lethal Apollon rain. Critics responded well: Rotten Tomatoes registered 82% positive from 33 reviews, with the critic consensus noting that the show 'starts out slow, but develops into a thrilling addition to the dystopia television genre.' Collider called it 'some of the best survivalist drama to hit screens in years.' IMDb audiences were cooler at 6.3 out of 10, a gap common to European genre series where critic enthusiasm outpaces casual viewer patience for character-first pacing.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Rain S01E01: "Stay Inside" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The first order is domestic. Go home. Stay there. A school day is already fraying, exam time is close, and panic arrives before anyone has the vocabulary for it. Then the rain becomes an instruction manual. Do not stand in it. Do not trust anyone who did. Do not open the door. "Stay Inside" works best when it turns survival into obedience, making every command feel sensible until it starts to feel like a cage. The premiere has a killer premise, a clean child-in-crisis engine, and a middle stretch that explains more than it threatens.

## The First Rule Is a Trap

The hour opens with urgency before it opens with apocalypse. Someone asks where she is, the reaction is a snapped "Fuck!", and exam pressure gives the first minutes a wonderfully ordinary panic. That matters. "Stay Inside" does not begin with grand disaster language. It begins with a family being late, a father issuing a command, and a daughter pulled out of normal life before she can understand the interruption.

**Dad** tells **Simone** to "Go home and stay there." As a line, it is plain. As the episode's operating system, it is everything. The premiere's smartest move is to make the central survival rule sound like something a parent would say on any bad day. The danger has not yet become mythic. It is still weather, traffic, news, confusion. Then the breaking report lands: heavy rainfall in Vordingborg is followed by symptoms. The world changes through bulletin logic, not spectacle.

That restraint gives the opening its bite. The rain is frightening because the episode refuses to make it abstract. It arrives as a forecast, a warning, a thing outside the window that adults suddenly treat like a predator. The problem is that Simone is asked to trust the rule before she is given the reason. That gap becomes the premiere's real tension. Safety depends on obedience, but obedience without explanation curdles into terror.

The opening also understands how quickly authority can shrink. Dad knows more than he says, yet his control over the situation is already slipping. His command carries parental force because Simone has no better option. That is the episode's cruel setup: a child is handed a rule that may save her life, then left with no adult who can explain when the rule bends, when it breaks, or what it costs.

## A Bunker That Sounds Like a Parent

The bunker sequence sharpens that idea. Inside, Dad's voice turns survival into procedure. Cleansing, standing still, staying sealed in. The space is built to protect **Rasmus** and Simone, but the episode films the safety system as cold ritual. A bunker should reassure. This one talks like a machine borrowing a parent's authority.

The command broadcast makes the show blunter in a useful way: "STAY INSIDE." The all-caps directness is the point. The phrase has the force of law. The warning about talking to people who went outside turns human contact into contamination, and that is where the episode's horror takes its nastiest shape. In most survival stories, another voice is hope. Here, another voice might be death asking politely to be let in.

The opened door aftermath is the hour's harshest emotional beat. After Dad is gone, Simone and others cry for help multiple times, and the episode lets that need rub against the rule. Someone outside might need saving. Someone inside might die if the rule breaks. It is a clean dilemma because neither side requires stupidity. Panic makes moral sense here.

Where the hour slips is in the amount of containment information it has to deliver. The midsection moves into an instruction-heavy rhythm: bunker systems, warnings, radio functions, emergency logic. The material is necessary, but the momentum softens when procedure replaces pressure for too long. The best scenes make the bunker feel like a loaded gun. A few passages make it feel like a manual.

That imbalance matters because the bunker is the episode's central set of contradictions. It is shelter, prison, schoolroom, quarantine chamber. The hour is strongest when those functions collide. The cleansing process feels practical until it becomes frighteningly impersonal. The sealed doors feel safe until someone outside begs. The systems feel designed for every emergency except the emotional emergency of two children left alone with rules they cannot interpret.

## Radio Hope Has a Cruel Signal

Simone's radio contact gives the episode its spine after the initial lockdown. Her introduction, "My name's Simone, and I'm with my brother Rasmus," is small, scared, and practical. That is why it lands. She is not making a heroic speech. She is trying to be found.

This is where **Mom**'s absence becomes more than tragedy. She wants Simone calm and safe inside, then dies outside, removing the one person who could translate adult emergency into child survival. Dad is missing. Mom is gone. The bunker can issue commands, but it cannot parent them. That gap is the emotional engine of the back half.

The radio thread also keeps Dad present without giving the hour the comfort of reunion. Simone wants to find him and reaches outward because the bunker is not enough. The story plants a hospital pick-up location and a possible rescue route, but it keeps interrupting hope with darkness, waiting, and blackout pressure. The episode understands that rescue is more suspenseful when it becomes another system that can fail.

The bleakest turn comes when the earlier hope of outside contact is answered by containment thinking: there is nothing out there. The line pushes the premiere away from rescue fantasy and toward abandonment. Still, the episode could have tightened this stretch. The waiting is thematically right, but some pauses sit in the same emotional register. Despair needs shape. A little more escalation inside the silence would have made the confinement cut deeper.

The radio also exposes Simone's growing role. She starts by asking for help, then becomes the person who has to judge whether help is real, delayed, or dangerous. That is a heavy shift, and the episode mostly handles it without overplaying her competence. Simone is frightened. She hesitates. She clings to instructions because they are the last trace of adult order. Her strength comes from staying usable under pressure, not from suddenly becoming fearless.

## Rasmus Opens the Wrong Door

Rasmus is the premiere's volatility engine. Simone's instinct is caution. Rasmus wants out. That contradiction is simple, but it gives the episode necessary movement once the bunker has established its rules. He goes outside despite warnings, after Simone insists it is too dangerous, and the choice does important character work. He acts like a child pushing against a world that has stopped explaining itself.

The episode needs that push. Without Rasmus, "Stay Inside" risks becoming a locked-room exercise in compliance. His desire to check what is out there turns the rule into a test. How long can a child treat invisible danger as real when every instinct says doors are made to open?

Simone's response makes her the premiere's clearest protagonist. She wants Dad, wants instructions, wants a plan, but she also becomes the person forced to act when the adults vanish. Her authority over Rasmus is improvised, not inherited. That makes it more interesting. She does not become brave because the plot needs a leader. She becomes functional because the alternative is letting the bunker, the rain, and her brother's fear decide everything.

Rasmus also gives the episode a necessary emotional counterweight. Simone can understand danger as instruction. Rasmus experiences it as deprivation. He is trapped away from his parents, separated from the world, and told that the outside has become lethal. His disobedience is reckless, but it is rooted in a recognizable child's logic: if no one will explain the danger, test the door. That makes the conflict sharper than a simple survival mistake.

The emergency override near the end is a good pressure beat because it weaponizes the system meant to protect them. Doors opening should mean rescue. Here, it means exposure. The premiere's best trick is that every solution carries the shape of a new danger.

## The Verdict

"Stay Inside" is a strong opener with one clean argument: survival begins as obedience, then obedience becomes its own horror. The episode earns that through Dad's command, the bunker ritual, Mom's death outside, Simone's radio reach, and Rasmus's need to break confinement. Its weakness is pacing. The middle stretch leans into information delivery and waiting in a way that occasionally dulls the dread it has built so well. Still, the premise is sharp, the family stakes are legible, and Simone emerges as a sturdy anchor for the season. As a first chapter, it plants the right questions: what the rain carries, where Dad has gone, and who guides these children once every adult system starts failing.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

episode_reviews.title: Trust Your Instincts
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale converges the siblings' search for their father with the Apollon corporation mystery. The show earns its cliffhanger by grounding it in character stakes rather than pure spectacle - what happens to Rasmus matters because eight episodes built toward it.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The revelation about Rasmus and the rain's real relationship to him - the season's central mystery snapping into place.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 returned in May 2019 with a tighter six-episode run that pushed deeper into the Apollon conspiracy and what Rasmus represents. The compressed episode order suited the mid-series revelations, though audience RT scores dropped from Season 1 levels. The season's character work - particularly Simone's evolving role as protector versus the group's view of her brother - gave the show continued emotional grounding.
seasons.season_over_season: The reduced six-episode count gives Season 2 a purposeful momentum Season 1's eight episodes occasionally lacked; the mythology deepens but audience scores reflected declining patience with the premise's unresolved center.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 concluded the series in August 2020 with another six-episode run. The RT audience score dropped to 36% for the final season, reflecting a common drop pattern for post-apocalyptic series that struggle to sustain mythology payoffs over three seasons. Netflix did not renew. The critical case for the show rests firmly on the first season.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 closes the story but the 36% RT audience score signals the mythology payoffs did not satisfy viewers who followed three seasons expecting answers - a common late-run penalty for mystery-box survivalist drama.
